title: ₹1 Crore and Empty Theatres on Day One — Three Weeks Later, Nobody Can Get a Ticket
excerpt: Imtiaz Ali's Partition romance Main Vaapas Aaunga has crossed ₹73 crore worldwide on pure word of mouth, with Sharvari delivering the performance of the summer — just days before she shows up in Alpha.
body:
The first day tells you everything — except when it doesn't.

<youtube></youtube>

When **Main Vaapas Aaunga** opened on June 12, it collected ₹1.15 crore. Not 115. Not 11.5. One point one five. In a summer where **Dhurandhar 2** opened to ₹145 crore and **Welcome To The Jungle** debuted at ₹19.4 crore, Imtiaz Ali's Partition love story arrived so quietly it was practically a whisper. Trade analysts had written their obituaries before the weekend even began.

Three weeks later, the film has crossed ₹73 crore worldwide. Its third Saturday — ₹4.25 crore — matched **Cocktail 2**'s *second* Saturday, despite opening at one-twelfth the size. People who didn't know the film existed in Week 1 are crying in theatres in Week 3. And **Imtiaz Ali** himself sounds almost bewildered.

> "This has all happened because of the audience and strong word of mouth. It is an overwhelming feeling and a matter of great joy. I am also a bit surprised." — Imtiaz Ali

He shouldn't be. This is exactly the kind of film he was born to make — and the kind Bollywood keeps forgetting it needs.

## A Promise That Survived 78 Years

**Main Vaapas Aaunga** — *I Will Return* — is a multi-generational love story set against the Partition of India. **Naseeruddin Shah** plays an elderly man on his deathbed, consumed by one unfulfilled promise: to return to Sargodha, the city he was torn from when the borders carved through Punjab in 1947. **Vedang Raina** plays his younger self, a boy desperately in love with Jiah, played by **Sharvari** — and the scenes between them have a tenderness that modern Bollywood rarely reaches for. Before being dragged across the new border, he tells her: *Main vaapas aaunga.*

Seventy-eight years later, it falls to his grandson — played by **Diljit Dosanjh**, magnetic and restrained — to honour that promise.

It's a film that asks a question the Indian diaspora understands in its bones: *What did we leave behind?* For the millions of families across Canada, the UK, the US, and the Gulf who carry Partition in their family stories, this isn't just cinema. It's a mirror held up to inherited grief.

## The Numbers That Defied Every Rule

The trajectory is almost unprecedented in modern Bollywood. An opening day of ₹1.15 crore typically means a film will struggle to reach ₹10 crore in its lifetime. Main Vaapas Aaunga simply rewrote the script:

- **Opening weekend**: ₹5.50 crore
- **First week**: ₹12.25 crore
- **Second weekend**: ₹12.10 crore — a staggering 120% jump over the first weekend
- **Day 18**: ₹47.80 crore net India, ₹73 crore worldwide

Against a reported budget of ₹70 crore, the film is now knocking on the door of profitability — a destination that seemed laughable a fortnight ago. In a summer dominated by **Dhurandhar 2** (₹1,850 crore), **Bhooth Bangla** (₹292 crore), and **Cocktail 2** (₹146 crore), this quiet Partition romance has earned its seat at the table on nothing but word of mouth. No franchise muscle. No universe it belongs to. Just a story, told beautifully.

And here's the detail that makes it even sweeter: **Diljit Dosanjh** famously kept his distance from the entire promotional cycle. No interviews. No press tours. No Koffee with Karan couches. He let the film speak for itself — and it screamed.

## The A.R. Rahman Reunion

You cannot talk about this film without talking about the music. **A.R. Rahman** and lyricist **Irshad Kamil** — reuniting with Imtiaz Ali in the creative trinity that gave us *Rockstar*, *Highway*, and *Tamasha* — have delivered a soundtrack that people are playing on loop and sending to everyone they know. The compositions don't just accompany the story; they *are* the story, the kind of soul-deep melodies that remind you why Rahman has no peers. Social media is full of people going to see the film specifically because a friend texted them a song.

**Mahesh Bhatt** himself drew comparisons to *Highway*, calling the film a deeply personal work that transcends its commercial reception. Coming from the man who made *Sadak* and *Arth*, that's not a throwaway compliment.

## Sharvari's Extraordinary Month

And then there's **Sharvari**, who is living the kind of month that most actors wouldn't dare dream of. Her performance as Jiah — a woman who carries an unfinished love story across a lifetime — is luminous, devastating, and exactly the kind of work that turns a rising star into a permanent one. The scenes where she silently processes losing everything she loves? You don't watch those. You *feel* them.

On **July 3** — just three days from now — she returns in a completely different skin as one of the leads in **Alpha**, the first female-led instalment in the YRF Spy Universe, alongside **Alia Bhatt** and **Bobby Deol**. From a Partition-era lover in pastels to a spy-universe warrior in tactical black. Within a single month. If Bollywood's 2026 has a breakout star, Sharvari isn't just in the conversation. She *is* the conversation.

## What This Film Proves

Main Vaapas Aaunga is the kind of film the industry celebrates after it succeeds and immediately forgets when it's time to greenlight the next slate. The lesson is right there, in neon: audiences are starving for emotional depth, for stories that trust silence over spectacle, for films where a single promise carries more weight than a ₹300-crore VFX budget.

But in a year where franchises and sequels have generated ₹3,000 crore at the domestic box office, the incentive to learn that lesson is exactly zero.

Still — for three weeks in the summer of 2026, a Partition love story reminded everyone what cinema is supposed to feel like. And Imtiaz Ali, the man who has spent a decade being told he's lost his touch, just proved that the touch was never the problem. The audience just needed to find him again.

*Main Vaapas Aaunga is currently playing in theatres across India, the US, Canada, the UK, Australia, and the Middle East.*
